channel.title: Parano1d Lab Research
channel.description: Papers, protocol work, reproducible engineering studies and results from Parano1d Lab.

item.title: Parano1d soundness under industry metrics
item.description: Committed production parameters evaluated under the metrics published by Plonky2, RISC Zero and ethSTARK, with conjectured scores separated from finite theorem-backed bounds.

item.title: FROST-GKR: a global trace protocol for batched Poseidon2b
item.description: A three-column committed trace reduces an entire batch of Poseidon2b executions with two constraint sumchecks.

item.title: Why HistoryStep uses two proof classes
item.description: HistoryStep is the recursive proof of a block's state transition. B64 handles up to 64 user transaction pages and meets the preparation budget on the reference laptop; B255 extends the same relation to the 255-page block limit. Measurements found no useful operating range for a third class.

item.title: Why a block is accepted only with its recursive proof
item.description: An early design accepted a block first and produced its recursive proof later in the background. The canonical chain could therefore move ahead of the HistoryStep-proven tip, forcing nodes to persist and recover a second queue. The production design accepts the block and its matching HistoryStep together: one atomic object, one canonical height and no deferred proof backlog.

item.title: Prove the block once, then search the nonce
item.description: HistoryStep binds every semantic header field under a nonce-free domain. PoW can vary the nonce without rebuilding the transition proof.

item.title: Bootstrapping from proof-carrying State
item.description: A joining node validates headers, verifies one recursive transition proof at a finalized boundary, installs exact live State and applies no more than eighteen recent blocks.

item.title: Replacing a consensus quarantine with UTXO incarnations
item.description: A monotone creation identifier inside the existing value lane invalidates stale slot openings without a second consensus root or reuse quarantine.

item.title: One proof format across four hardware paths
item.description: PCLMUL, VPCLMUL, AVX-512 and PMULL execute the same GF(2¹²⁸) arithmetic without changing witness layout or proof bytes.

item.title: One global Poseidon walk replaces nine verifier walks
item.description: A full-composition benchmark showed that independent verifier walks multiplied memory beyond 30 GB. One shared domain removed that factor.

item.title: The recursive verifier had to fit inside itself
item.description: A class with a 2^23-position constraint domain closes recursively: each proof verifies a predecessor with the same authenticated matrix and public layout.

item.title: AuthStream: bounding a block-wide authorization workload
item.description: Streaming compilation bounded 14–16 MiB of private authorization data with 4.7% overhead. The evaluated terminal proof did not meet the production latency budget.

item.title: The proof got 20% smaller and 68% slower
item.description: Fusing two Merkle relations saved 5.94 KB but enlarged the combined multilinear trace and removed parallelism. Proving regressed from 2.68 to 4.50 seconds.

item.title: One owner, one authorization proof
item.description: Public transaction arithmetic belongs to the block relation. The wallet proves one private fact—ownership—even when a spend contains 1,020 inputs.

item.title: Source binding for compact mixed openings
item.description: An A/A′ adversarial test separates low-degree consistency from commitment provenance. A source root and shared queries close the edge.

item.title: Three polynomial-commitment experiments and the bottlenecks they exposed
item.description: Ladder FRI exposed proof-byte cost, FRI-Binius exposed source binding, and BaseFold exposed the cost of putting a verifier inside its successor.
